questions.question: Discuss how human activities impact decomposers in an ecosystem. / [CO1]

  • Human activities including deforestation, mining, urbanisation, pollution due to pesticides

  • decomposers to thrive. (LiberalValuation)

questions.question: Distinguish between food chain and food web with examples. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Distinguishbetweenfoodchainandfoodwebwithexamples. U/CO1
  • A food chain is a linear sequence of organisms in an ecosystem, where each organism
  • serves as a source of food (energy) for the next organism in the chain. It illustrates the flow of
  • energy and nutrients through an ecosystem, starting with primary producers and moving up
  • through consumers.
  • Example 1:Grass→Grasshopper→Frog→Snake→Hawk (terrestrial)
  • Example 2: Phytoplankton→Zooplankton→SmallFish→Tuna→Shark (aquatic).
  • A food web is a more complex and realistic representation of the feeding relationships in
  • an ecosystem compared to a food chain. While a food chain shows a linear sequence, a food web
  • illustrates how different food chains in an ecosystem are interconnected, showing the many
  • pathways through which energy and nutrients flow.
  • Example: In a forest ecosystem whereplants are eaten byrabbits,squirrels,andinsects,
  • which are then consumed byfoxes,snakes,andhawks.
  • (Any two distinguishing features with any one example for each, give full credit)

  • moderate offspring number. Equal chance of dying at any age. Graph is a Straight line.

questions.question: Differentiate between absolute natality and ecological natality. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Differentiatebetweenabsolutenatalityandecologicalnatality. U/CO2
  • Absolute Natality: The maximum number of new individuals an organism can produce
  • under ideal conditions.
  • EcologicalNatality: The increase in population size under real, environmental conditions.

questions.question: Compare intraspecific competition and interspecific competition. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Compareintraspecificcompetitionandinterspecificcompetition. [U]/[CO2]
  • Ans: Intraspecific: Competition among individuals of the same species.
  • Interspecific: Competition between individuals of different species.
  • Both affect resource availability and population dynamics. (Definition-1 mark each; example. for
  • each- 0.5 mark each/ the impact of competition- 0.5 mark).

questions.question: Describe exponential growth curve. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Describeexponentialgrowthcurve. U/CO2
  • In exponential population growth, the population increases at a constant rate over time,
  • assuming there are unlimited resources and no environmental limitations. The growth rate is
  • directly proportional to the current population size resulting in a J-shaped curve when represents
  • in a graph. This curve usually does not flatten out, though some models may show the growth rate
  • slowing down as the population approaches the environment’s carrying capacity

questions.question: Identify the key goals of the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF). / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• IdentifythekeygoalsoftheWorldWideFundforNature(WWF). [U]/[CO3]
  • Ans: Conservation or Protection of biodiversity. Sustainable use of renewable natural resources.
  • Reduction of pollution and wasteful consumption. Fair and equitable sharing of benefits(Anythree)

questions.question: Examine the role of women in the Chipko Movement. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• ExaminetheroleofwomenintheChipkoMovement. U/CO3
  • Chipko Movement identified chiefly as a women movement, originated in the Garhwal
  • Himalayan Mountain region of the Uttarakhand state in 1970s. Its aim was to prevent
  • deforestation and conserve forests. Mira Behn and Goura Devi were the women leaders of the
  • movement. Women act as the primary agents of change by pioneering the strategy of hugging
  • trees (Chipko) to prevent deforestation. As they depended on forests for fodder, firewood, and
  • water, local women led by figures like Gaura Devi led protests to protect their livelihood from
  • commercial exploitation. The movement became a platform for rural women to emerge as
  • community leaders, shifting from traditional roles to active political protestors (Women
  • empowerment and social change).

questions.question: Summarize the highlights of G20 Summit 2023. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:

questions.question: List 3 types of human activities allowed in wildlife sanctuaries. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:

  • • Private ownership rights
  • • Timber harvesting
  • • Collecting minor forest products: Gathering honey, fruits, berries, and medicinal

  • • Regulated Eco-tourism: Wildlife photography, safaris, and bird watching.
  • • Sustainable Resource Use: Regulated grazing of livestock and, in some cases,

questions.question: Discuss the impact of overexploitation on biodiversity. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Discusstheimpactofoverexploitationonbiodiversity. [U]/[CO3]
  • Ans: Population declines; species extinction and habitat destruction. Disruption of ecosystem
  • balance- less resilient ecosystem. Loss of species thereby reducing genetic diversity/biodiversity.
  • (Any 2 with explanation. 1.5 mark each).

questions.question: India is a mega-diversity nation. Explain. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Indiaisamega-diversitynation.Explain. U/CO3
  • Nearly 7-8% of the recorded species are present in India. 4 of the 34 globally identified
  • biodiversity hotspots are there. India is a vast repository of traditional knowledge associated with
  • biological resources. Over 91,200 animal species and 45,500 plant species have been documented
  • in the ten biogeographic regions of the country. Along with species richness, India also possesses
  • high rates of endemism. Wide range of ecosystems and habitats are present due to varied climatic,
  • topographic and geological conditions. India has vast coastline and associated wetlands which
  • holds wide varieties of rare and endangered species too. Nine biosphere reserves, six ‘Ramsar
  • sites’ and five ‘World Heritage Sites’ are also present in India.

questions.question: Outline the primary goals of establishing biosphere reserves. / [CO3] [3x6 = 18]
questions.solution_html:

questions.question: Interpret what a high Simpson’s index value reveals about a community. / [CO3] [3x6 = 18]
questions.solution_html:
• InterpretwhatahighSimpson’sIndexvaluerevealsaboutacommunity. U/CO3
  • A high value in Simpson’s Index of Diversity (1-D) reveals a community with high
  • biodiversity, characterized by a large number of species and a relatively even distribution of
  • individuals among those species. It indicates high species richness, high species evenness,
  • ecosystem stability and resilience and no dominance of any species.
  • (3X6=18Marks)
  • PartC
  • Each question carries 5 marks

questions.question: Energy flow in an ecosystem is unidirectional. Justify. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Energyflowinanecosystemisunidirectional.Justify. [U] / [CO1]
  • Ans: Define energy flow. Energy flows from sun → producers → consumers → decomposers.
  • Cannot be reused by the previous trophic level. Energy cannot be destroyed (1st Law) Loss of energy
  • at each step as heat (Second Law of Thermodynamics). Ensures ecosystem stability.
  • (Define energy flow-1 mark. Explain energy flow- 1 mark. Thermodynamics principles- 2 mark, 1
  • example- 1 mark)

questions.question: Discuss the roles of bacteria in maintaining the nitrogen cycle. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Discusstheroleofbacteriainmaintainingthenitrogencycle. U/CO1
  • Bacteria are crucial for maintaining the environmental balance of nitrogen. They drive the
  • transformation of nitrogen into different chemical forms through nitrogen fixation (Rhizobium,
  • Acetobacter), nitrification (Nitrosomonas, Nitrobacter), ammonification, and denitrification
  • (Pseudomonas, Clostridium). Without these microorganisms, nitrogen would accumulate in
  • unusable forms (nitrites), leading to decreased soil fertility and limiting plant growth. They are
  • also essential in wastewater treatment and agriculture, providing natural fertilization.
  • (Brief explanation of nitrifying process, give full credit)

questions.question: Explain the concept of community stratification in ecological systems. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Explaintheconceptofcommunitystratificationinecologicalsystems.(Liberal Valuaution)
  • [U] / [CO2]
  • Ans: Vertical layering of plants and animals.
  • Improves use of light, water, nutrients. Reduces direct competition.
  • Examples: Canopy, small trees and shrubs, shrub layer, forest floor with decomposers and small
  • animals in forests (terrestrial ecosystems).
  • In aquatic (floating plants on top, submerged plants below, and bottom-dwelling creatures).

questions.question: Compare and differentiate keystone species and umbrella species. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Compareanddifferentiatekeystonespeciesandumbrellaspecies U/CO2
  • Keystone Species: The species that have an extremely high impact on a particular
  • ecosystem relative to its population. The removal of a keystone species from a habitat results in a
  • dramatic change in the habitat. These species affect the structure and function of an ecosystem
  • and the plant and animal species residing in that ecosystem. E.g., Sea otters, Beavers
  • Umbrella Species: The species which has a habitat that is important to the survival of
  • many other animals. An umbrella species provide protection to a wide range of other species and
  • their habitats. These species are often selected for conservation efforts because their survival
  • inherently safeguards ecosystems and biodiversity. E.g., Giant Panda, Asian Elephant

questions.question: Describe the key legal provisions under the Biological Diversity Act, 2002. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:

  • Ans: Conservation of biological diversity. Sustainable use of biological resources. Fair and equitable
  • sharing of benefits. Establishment of National Biodiversity Authority (NBA).
  • Regulation of access to genetic resources. (Brief description of anyfive).

questions.question: Assess how the UN’s Sustainable Development Goal 15 of the 2030 Agenda addresses biodiversity loss and ecosystem restoration. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Assess how the UN’s Sustainable Development Goal 15 of the 2030 Agenda addresses
  • biodiversitylossandecosystemrestoration. An/CO3
  • UN Sustainable Development Goal 15 (SDG 15) serves as a critical, actionable framework
  • to “Life on Land” by aiming to protect, restore, and promote sustainable terrestrial ecosystems by
  • 2030. The SDGs are structured around five pillars: People, Planet, Prosperity, Peace and
  • Partnerships.
  • It addresses biodiversity loss by focusing on:
  • • Conserving, restoring and using terrestrial ecosystems in a sustainable manner
  • • Fighting against desertification
  • • Rehabilitating degraded lands and soils
  • • Conserving mountain ecosystems, including their biological diversity
  • • Taking measures to end poaching and trafficking of protected flora and fauna.

questions.question: Describe the origin and impact of the Chipko Movement. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• DescribetheoriginandimpactoftheChipkoMovement. [U] / [CO3]
  • Ans: Started in 1973, former Uttar Pradesh portion. Issue- massive felling of tress as a consequence
  • of urbanisation. Forests- source of livelihood for villagers, role in flood control/ landslides. Villagers
  • (women) hugged trees- a non-violent act- to stop commercial deforestation. Led by Sunderlal
  • Bahuguna. Increased forest conservation awareness and prevented deforestation. Influenced India's
  • forest protection policies.

questions.question: Examine how biodiversity conservation benefits human society and provide examples. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Examinehowbiodiversityconservationbenefitshumansocietyandprovideexamples.
  • A/CO3
  • Biodiversity conservation benefits human society in many direct and indirect ways.
  • Biodiversity includes the variety of plants, animals, microorganisms, and ecosystems on Earth.
  • Protecting it helps maintain ecological balance and supports human life, health, and economies.
  • The benefits for humans by biodiversity includes:
  • • Provides food and medicines (Crops, Livestock, medicines derived from plants, fungi, and
  • microorganisms)
  • • Maintains ecosystems services (Clean air and water, Soil fertility, Pollination, Flood
  • control, Climate regulation)
  • • Supports economic development (by means of ecotourism, forest products, sustainable
  • fishing etc.)
  • • Protects against natural disasters and climate change (Coral reefs protect coastlines,
  • Forests reduce landslides and regulate rainfall, Diverse agricultural systems are better able
  • to survive droughts and pests)
  • • Preserves cultural and recreational values
  • • Ensures scientific and future benefits
  • (Points with brief explanation and example, give full credit)

questions.question: Identify the key policies and regulations related to watershed management in India. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• IdentifythekeypoliciesandregulationsrelatedtowatershedmanagementinIndia.
  • [U] / [CO4]
  • Ans: Focus on soil conservation, water harvesting, afforestation, land use management. Promotes
  • community participation. Helps in improving rural livelihoods and agriculture.
  • Construction of check dams, percolation tanks, dug-out ponds. Multicropping to promote
  • sustainability and control soil run-off. Government policies like mandatory water harvesting
  • structures in every new building.
  • Drought Prone Areas Programme (DPAP), Desert Development Programme (DPP), Integrated
  • wasteland Development Programme (IWDP), Haryali project, Neeru-Meeru, Arvani Pani Sansad.
  • (Either the specific initiatives OR the strategies- 5)

questions.question: Explain how the Forest Conservation Act, 1980, protects forest areas from unauthorized use or destruction. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• ExplainhowtheForestConservationAct,1980,protectsforestareasfromunauthoriseduse
  • ordestruction. U/CO4
  • The Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 was enacted by the Government of India to protect
  • forests from deforestation, illegal diversion, and non-forest activities. The Act places strict
  • controls on the use of forest land and helps conserve biodiversity and ecological balance.
  • The main ways by which the Act protects Forest Areas are as follows:
  • • The State Government need mandatory approval from the Central Government for forest
  • land use prevents uncontrolled clearing of forests for industries, mining, roads, dams, or
  • commercial projects.
  • • Restricts non-forest activities like mining, commercial agriculture, industrial expansion etc.
  • • Prevents deforestation which helps to protect wildlife habitats, maintain rainfall and
  • climate balance etc.
  • • Compensatory afforestation
  • • Penal action against violations
  • • Supports wildlife and biodiversity conservation
